original_summary: Mariáš is a Czech three-player trick-taking game with a 32-card deck. In each deal one declarer chooses trump and a contract and plays alone against two defenders who work as a partnership. Points come from Aces, Tens, the last trick and King-Ober marriages, and the game adds doubling (Flek), stakes doubled for Hearts as trump, and special contracts (Betl, Durch, 7, 100).

review.evidence: No simple policy wins. Always bidding high fails contracts, and always passing leaves the eldest stuck with weak forced games. The declarer role rotates, so no seat has a built-in edge. Card choices decide tricks.

Judging hand strength, choosing trump, cooperating on defence and counting cards all reliably beat naive play over many deals. Card luck within a single deal is large, but it averages out across a session.
Inferring the unseen hands, timing trumps and protecting Tens is never fully solved. A weak player still scores when they hold strong cards.
Hands are hidden. Players must infer the other holdings from the bid and the cards played, defenders must coordinate without talking, and the declarer must plan over 10 tricks.
Card points, marriages and contract success are all arithmetic.

There are 32 cards, 10 tricks and several deals, so the game runs far past 40 rounds. The talon exchange, Flek/Re chains and four special contracts with their own rules are conditional blocks the flat step list cannot hold. Legality and marriage checks also exceed the step budget.

problems: P1: The original is too long and too branchy for the platform: 32 cards, 10 tricks, a talon exchange, a Flek/Re doubling dialogue and four special contracts (Betl, Durch, 7, 100) that each need their own block of rules.

P2: The previous variation understated its step budget. Its real count was about 24 steps per round, above the limit of 20, because trick-winner computation, marriage detection and end-of-deal scoring were not compacted.
P3: The previous fallback for an illegal card ('lowest-ranked legal card') had no tie-break when several legal cards share a rank in different suits.
P4: The previous variation had no rule for an invalid bid value or a missing or invalid trump suit, so trump could be undefined, for example when the eldest submitted PASS without a suit.
P5: The previous variation claimed 20 attributes, at the cap, without listing them, so feasibility was not shown.
P6: The previous legality rule 'if no trump has yet been played' was ambiguous when trump itself is led.

changes.what: Keep the 20-card, 6-trick, 6-deal match (36 rounds). Use a single numeric contract with a sealed simultaneous bid. Drop Flek, the special contracts and the talon exchange; the talon stays as unseen dead cards.
changes.why: This keeps bidding, trump choice, marriages, partnership defence and the Hearts doubling while fitting 36 rounds with no conditional blocks.
changes.fixes: P1: The original is too long and too branchy for the platform.

changes.what: Encode every card as a number, code = suit*5 + rank (suits Hearts=0, Bells=1, Leaves=2, Acorns=3; ranks U=0, O=1, K=2, 10=3, A=4). The trick winner is the card with the maximum key = rank + 10*(is trump) + 5*(is led suit), computed in one calc step. Marriages for all players are found in one calc step at bidding. Tally, S, the fail transform, Hearts doubling and the score update are merged into one calc step. Give an explicit 18-step list.
changes.why: This brings the real step count to 18, within the limit of 20.
changes.fixes: P2: The previous variation understated its step budget.

changes.what: Fallback for an illegal card: the legal card with the lowest rank; among equal ranks, the first in the suit order Hearts, Bells, Leaves, Acorns.
changes.why: This makes the fallback a single, fully determined card.
changes.fixes: P3: The previous fallback had no tie-break.

changes.what: A bid not in the list counts as PASS. The eldest's PASS or invalid bid counts as 50. A missing or invalid suit defaults to the suit in which that bidder holds the most cards, ties broken by the suit order Hearts, Bells, Leaves, Acorns.
changes.why: Contract and trump are now always defined.
changes.fixes: P4: The previous variation had no rule for an invalid bid or suit.

changes.what: List the attributes explicitly. Use one list of the cards in the current trick instead of separate led-suit, best-card, winner and trick-points attributes. Derive the defenders' trick count as (tricks completed − declarer's tricks), and derive the eldest from the round number. The total is 16.
changes.why: This shows feasibility with headroom under the cap of 20.
changes.fixes: P5: The previous variation claimed 20 attributes without listing them.

changes.what: Restate the follow rule: if you hold the led suit you must play it, and you must beat the highest card of the led suit in the trick if you can. The beating duty is lifted only when the led suit is not trump and a trump has already been played to the trick.
changes.why: This removes the ambiguity when trump is led.
changes.fixes: P6: The previous legality rule was ambiguous when trump is led.

keeps: A lone declarer against a two-player defending partnership, chosen anew each deal.
The rank order A, 10, K, O, U, with Aces and Tens worth 10 each and 10 for the last trick.
The duties to follow suit, to beat the trick (head it) and to trump.
King+Ober marriages worth 40 in trump and 20 otherwise, counting only if the holder's side wins a trick.
A contract the declarer must reach, with a heavier penalty for failing.
Doubled stakes when Hearts are trump.
The eldest hand rotating and obliged to play if nobody bids.

recommendation.reason: The cut-down 20-card game keeps the essence of Mariáš (bidding, trump, marriages, partnership defence, hidden hands) and now fits the platform's limits with an explicit step and attribute list.

variation.name: Little Bidding Mariáš
variation.summary: A 3-player, 20-card Mariáš played over 6 deals of 6 tricks. Each deal opens with a sealed simultaneous bid for the contract and trump suit. The highest bidder plays alone against the other two, trying to reach the contract with card points and marriages.
variation.rules:
CARDS. There are 20 cards in four suits, Hearts, Bells, Leaves and Acorns, each with ranks A, 10, K, O (Ober) and U (Unter). Within a suit the ranks run from highest to lowest A, 10, K, O, U. Each Ace and each Ten is worth 10 card points; all other cards are worth 0. Winning the 6th (last) trick of a deal is worth 10 more points, so the deal has 90 card points in total. Internally each card has the code suit*5 + rank, with suits Hearts=0, Bells=1, Leaves=2, Acorns=3 and ranks U=0, O=1, K=2, 10=3, A=4. Players see and name cards by their names, for example 'Ten of Leaves'. Suit order for tie-breaks is Hearts, Bells, Leaves, Acorns.

MATCH. The match has 6 deals of 6 tricks each, 36 rounds in total. Each round is one trick. Players are seated P1, P2, P3, and seat order is cyclic (P1, P2, P3, P1, ...). The eldest is P1 in deals 1 and 4, P2 in deals 2 and 5, and P3 in deals 3 and 6. Every score starts at 0. Players may not exchange messages at any time; defenders cooperate only through their card play.

DEAL (first round of each deal). The engine shuffles all 20 cards and deals 6 to each player privately. The remaining 2 cards are the talon: face down, seen by no one, and out of play for the whole deal.

BIDDING (first round of each deal, one simultaneous poll). Every player privately submits one answer containing a bid and a suit. A bid is PASS or one of 50, 60, 70, 80, 90, 100, 110, 120, 130, 140, 150. A suit is Hearts, Bells, Leaves or Acorns.
- Any bid not in this list counts as PASS.
- The eldest may not pass: an eldest PASS or invalid bid counts as 50.
- A missing or invalid suit becomes the suit in which that player holds the most cards, ties broken by the suit order.
All bids and suits are then revealed together. The highest bid wins. If bids are equal, the eldest wins the tie first, then the next player in seat order after the eldest. The winner is the declarer, their bid is the contract T, and their suit is trump. The other two players are the defenders and form a team for this deal.

MARRIAGES (announced right after bidding). Every player who holds both the K and the O of one suit has a marriage in that suit. A marriage is worth 40 in the trump suit and 20 in any other suit, and it belongs to its holder's side (declarer or defenders). The engine publicly announces every marriage, its holder and its value. At the end of the deal a side's marriages count only if that side won at least one trick.

PLAYING A TRICK. The declarer leads the first trick of the deal. After that, the winner of the previous trick leads. Starting with the leader, each player in seat order plays one card, and each card is announced to all. The leader may play any card. For the other players:
(a) If you hold a card of the led suit, you must play that suit. You must also play one that beats the highest card of the led suit already in the trick, if you can. This beating duty is lifted only when the led suit is not trump and a trump has already been played to this trick.
(b) If you hold no card of the led suit but hold a trump, you must play a trump. It must beat the highest trump already in the trick, if you can.
(c) Otherwise you may play any card.
If a player names a card that is illegal or not in their hand, the engine plays for them the legal card of lowest rank; among equal ranks, the first in the suit order.
The trick is won by the highest trump in it, or by the highest card of the led suit if it holds no trump. Equivalently, each card gets the key rank + 10 if it is trump + 5 if it is of the led suit, and the highest key wins. The card points of the trick, plus 10 if it is the 6th trick, go to the winner's side: the declarer alone, or the defenders together. The engine announces the trick winner and both sides' running points.

END OF DEAL (after the 6th trick).
1. The declarer's tally is the declarer's points (including any last-trick 10), plus the declarer's marriages if the declarer won at least 1 trick, minus the defenders' marriages if the defenders won at least 1 trick.
2. Let S = (T − 40) / 10, so a contract of 50 gives S = 1 and 150 gives S = 11.
3. If the tally is at least T, the contract is made and S is unchanged. Otherwise S becomes −(S + 1).
4. If trump is Hearts, S is doubled.
5. The declarer's score changes by 2×S, and each defender's score changes by −S.
6. The engine announces the tally, whether the contract was made, and all scores.

ENGINE STEP LIST (per round; steps marked [trick 1] run only in the first round of a deal, and steps marked [trick 6] only in the last).
1. [trick 1] Shuffle and deal 6 hidden cards to each player and 2 to the talon.
2. [trick 1] Reset the declarer's points, the defenders' points and the declarer's tricks to 0.
3. [trick 1] Simultaneous poll: bid and suit.
4. [trick 1] Calc: apply the invalid-input rules; set declarer, T, trump, and leader = declarer.
5. [trick 1] Calc: the marriage values of the declarer's side and of the defenders' side.
6. [trick 1] Announce the bids, declarer, contract, trump and marriages.
7. Clear the list of cards in the current trick.
8. The leader chooses a card.
9. Validate or apply the fallback; remove the card from the hand, add it to the trick list, announce it.
10. The next player chooses a card.
11. Validate, remove, add and announce as in step 9.
12. The third player chooses a card.
13. Validate, remove, add and announce as in step 9.
14. Calc the trick winner by maximum key. Add the trick points (+10 on trick 6) to the winner's side, add 1 to the declarer's tricks if the declarer won, set the leader to the winner, and announce.
15. [trick 6] Calc the tally, S, the fail transform, Hearts doubling and all score changes.
16. [trick 6] Announce the tally, the result and the scores.
17. Advance the round counter.
18. [round 36] End the match and decide the winner.

ATTRIBUTES (16). Per player (4): score, hand, bid, bid suit. Table (12): round number, talon, declarer, contract T, trump, leader, cards in the current trick, declarer's points, defenders' points, declarer's tricks, declarer-side marriage value, defender-side marriage value. The deal number, trick number and eldest are derived from the round number. The defenders' trick count is (tricks completed − declarer's tricks).
variation.objective: After round 36 (6 deals), the player with the highest total score wins. If two or three players tie for the highest total, the game is a draw. Every deal is zero-sum (the declarer gains 2×S, and each defender loses S), so the totals always sum to 0.
variation.expected_effect: The sealed simultaneous bid makes each player weigh their own hand against what the others might hold. They must also guess whether a rival will outbid them, because overbidding is punished by the extra −1 on failure and by doubling under Hearts. The eldest's forced 50 rewards careful trump choice and good declarer play with weak cards. Defenders must coordinate through their card play alone: signalling by the suits they discard, saving Tens, and timing the last trick. Simple policies lose. Always bidding 150 fails essentially every time, at −24 or worse per deal. Always passing leaves the eldest exposed to forced 50 contracts and hands every profitable contract to the opponents. Always naming Hearts doubles losses as much as gains. Each player is eldest twice, so seats are balanced. There is no talk: the only conflict is between the declarer and the defending team, the defenders share one objective, and messages would only allow illegal signalling.

balanced.evidence:
Score changes are zero-sum: declarer 2S and each defender -S. Payoffs per contract (non-Hearts; Hearts doubles all):
50 (S=1): made +2/-1/-1; failed S=-2, so -4/+2/+2. Declarer breaks even at p(make)=4/6=0.667.
60 (S=2): +4/-2/-2 vs -6/+3/+3. Break-even p=0.60.
100 (S=6): +12/-6/-6 vs -14/+7/+7. Break-even p=0.54.
150 (S=11): +22/-11/-11 vs -24/+12/+12. Break-even p=0.52.
Feasibility: there are 80 card points plus 10 for the last trick. On average the talon removes 2*8/20*10 = 8 points, leaving about 82 in play. A player holds a K+O pair in some suit with probability of roughly 0.3; naming that suit trump is worth +40. So 50 is makeable with a trump marriage or 2-3 high cards and long trumps, and doubtful otherwise.
Thoughtless policies under the winner rule:
- Always 150: almost never reaches a tally of 150, which needs 90 card points plus about 60 in marriages. It loses about 24 per deal won and loses the match against any opponent.
- Always PASS: as eldest it is forced to 50 with a random hand, likely below the 0.667 break-even, so it bleeds. As a defender it gains only when others fail. Against a sensible bidder who declares strong hands for +4 to +12, it loses on average. It does not 'never lose'.
- Random bidding: frequent overbids at large negative values; loses.
No bid or suit is strictly better whatever the opponents hold or do. Hearts doubles both the gain and the loss, so it is a risk choice, not a dominant one.
Seat edge: the eldest has the forced bid and tie priority, and eldest duty rotates exactly twice per seat over 6 deals, so this is symmetric. P3 being forced eldest in the final deal is a small positional quirk but not decisive. All three players can realistically win, and the defenders' shared interest is real for each deal.

playable.evidence:
Card count is consistent: 3*6+2 = 20, with 6 tricks per deal and 36 rounds (within 40). The game is finite and decided by arithmetic. The choice steps per round are 1 bid poll + 3 card plays = 4, which is at the limit. Hidden elements (hands, talon) = 2. There is one shuffle per deal, so random draws stay within 1 per round.
No talk is a sensible choice. The only disagreement is in the simultaneous bid, and defenders share one objective, so talk would be copying or illegal signalling.
Problems:
(1) Step budget is understated. Because the step list is flat, every round carries all steps guarded by `when`: shuffle; deal to 3 hidden hands (about 2 steps); bid poll; resolve the highest bid with rotating tie priority (about 2); marriage detection for 3 players x 4 suits with ownership, which needs calc or a referee and is announced (about 2); 3 card plays with legality and fallback (3); trick-winner computation (trump > led suit > rank) with no lookup operation (about 2-3, similar to the matrix workaround); assign points and count tricks per side (about 2); end-of-deal last-trick bonus, tally with conditional marriages, S, fail transform, Hearts doubling, score update and announcement (about 6). That is about 24, well above the stated 12 and above the limit of 20.
(2) The fallback 'lowest-ranked legal card' has no tie-break when several legal cards share a rank in different suits, for example two Unters when discarding freely.
(3) There is no rule for an invalid bid (for example 55 or 160) or a missing or invalid suit, which matters for an eldest who submits PASS without a suit, since trump would be undefined.
(4) The attribute count of 20 is at the cap with no listed attributes. Per-side tricks won, the led suit, the current best card and trick winner, the trump-played flag, contract, trump, declarer, eldest, both sides' points, both sides' marriages and 3 scores leave no headroom, so feasibility must be shown.

reasoning_over_luck.evidence:
The deal is a large factor. Over only 6 deals, hand strength and marriages decide much of who can declare profitably. I estimate about 50% of the match outcome is due to chance.
Skill clearly matters, though:
- Bidding to the right level is worth a lot. Break-even rises toward 0.52 at high contracts, an overbid by 10 costs extra points, and the Hearts choice doubles exposure.
- Simultaneous revealed bids and public marriages leak hand information.
- Only 18 cards are live and every card is announced, so counting and inferring the two unseen talon cards is feasible.
- Defenders must coordinate through play without talk.
With all players playing well, results still vary with the deal but are not decided by the draw alone. A good player bids to make and declines unsound contracts. A poor player who overbids or misplays trumps loses heavily, because a failed contract costs more than a made one gains (-(S+1) vs S). There is a clear thing to infer and a way to act on it.

required_changes: Provide an explicit step list that fits steps_per_round <= 20. For example, encode each card as a number (suit*5 + rank) so the trick winner is one calc step: key = rank + 10*isTrump + 5*isLedSuit, take the max. Compute all marriages in one referee or calc step at bidding. Merge the end-of-deal tally, S, fail transform, Hearts doubling and score update into at most 3 calc steps.
List the attributes and show they number at most 20.
Give the illegal-card fallback a full tie-break, e.g. 'lowest rank; among equal ranks, the first in the suit order Hearts, Bells, Leaves, Acorns'.

Define handling of invalid input in the bid poll: a bid not in the list counts as PASS (as 50 for the eldest). A missing or invalid suit defaults to the suit in which the bidder holds the most cards, with ties broken by the fixed suit order, so trump is always defined.

balanced.evidence:
SCORING TABLE. S = (T-40)/10. Declarer gets +2S if made and -2(S+1) if failed. Each defender gets the negative of half that. Hearts doubles everything.

| T | made: declarer / each defender | failed: declarer / each defender |
|---|---|---|
| 50 | +2 / -1 | -4 / +2 |
| 80 | +8 / -4 | -10 / +5 |
| 150 | +22 / -11 | -24 / +12 |

At 50 the declarer must make the contract more than 2/3 of the time to break even (EV = 6p - 4).

TRICK KEY. Off-suit 0-4, led suit 5-9, trump 10-14, trump led 15-19. Every card has a distinct code, so a trick can never tie. The key matches the stated trick rule.

THOUGHTLESS POLICIES, by the winner rule.
(1) Always bid 150. This player declares in almost every deal, because a 150 bid is only tied by another 150, and ties go to the eldest. A 150 tally needs about 90 card points plus 60 or more in marriages, which is practically impossible: 6 cards cannot hold 3 marriages and also 80 card points. Each deal costs -24 against +12 for each opponent, so this policy loses to every opponent policy.
(2) Always pass. As eldest, a pass counts as 50, so this player is forced to declare 50 in their two eldest deals with no hand-based judgement. As a non-eldest, they defend. Against a sensible bidder who bids only with strong hands (long trump, Aces and Tens, marriages), the contract is usually made and the passer loses 1 to 11 points per deal. The passer then ends below the sensible player. Passing is not dominant, and the policy loses against sensible play.
(3) Always bid 50. This player declares whenever the others pass, and often fails at 50 with a random hand. On average they hold 2.4 of the 8 point cards, and two defenders hold more of the trumps. Against sensible play this loses.
(4) Always Hearts. This doubles losses as well as gains, so it is only good when the contract is likely to be made. It is not strictly better.

NO STRICTLY BETTER OPTION. In every bid/suit and card choice, the best action depends on the hand and on the others' choices.

SEAT EDGE. Being eldest is forced and loses ties. Each seat is eldest exactly twice (deals 1/4, 2/5, 3/6), and the tie order rotates with the eldest, so the match is seat-symmetric. The declarer's lead is balanced by the 2-on-1 defence.

TOTALS. The game is zero-sum: 2S - S - S = 0. Defenders share identical changes, so their interests within a deal are aligned and there is no late-round betrayal temptation. All three players can realistically win.

playable.evidence:
COMPLETENESS. The rules cover every situation a model needs:
- Card names, ranks and points are defined.
- Talon handling is defined.
- Bid list, invalid-bid fallback, forced eldest 50 and invalid-suit fallback are defined.
- Bid ties are resolved by eldest, then seat order.
- Marriages: values, ownership, public announcement, and the at-least-one-trick condition are defined.
- Card play: follow suit, beat the highest led card, the exemption once a trump is in a non-trump-led trick, must trump and overtrump, otherwise free.
- The illegal-card fallback is deterministic: lowest rank, then suit order.
- The trick winner is computed by key; the leader is the previous winner.
- The tally, fail transform, Hearts doubling, score changes and the final winner/draw rule are all arithmetic on numbers the game keeps.

FINITE. Fixed at 36 rounds.

LIMITS. All within bounds:

| Limit | Value | Maximum |
|---|---|---|
| steps_per_round | 18 | 20 |
| choice_steps_per_round (1 simultaneous poll + 3 card choices) | 4 | 4 |
| attributes | 16 | 20 |
| hidden_elements (hands, talon) | 2 | 3 |
| random_draws_per_round (shuffle only in trick 1) | 1 | 1 |
| rounds | 36 | 40 |

The card-legality check is a complex rule check, which the platform allows a referee to rule on. There is no board, clock or trading, and no conditional block is needed: per-step [trick 1] and [trick 6] conditions are single-step `when` gates.

SIMULTANEOUS CHOICES. Bidding is one simultaneous poll, as required.

TALK. There is no talk, which is a sensible decision. Any defender talk would be public, so the declarer would read it. Bids are sealed and simultaneous, so cheap talk before them adds words rather than a real decision. The players do disagree, but they have plenty to reason about from the revealed bids, the marriage announcements and the public card play. Coordination through card play is the traditional and intended challenge.

reasoning_over_luck.evidence:
WHAT THERE IS TO INFER.
- Opponents' hands, from their revealed bids and bid suits. A non-eldest bidding 70 signals a long suit or point cards.
- Marriage announcements, which reveal Kings and Obers.
- Every played card, plus the 2 unknown talon cards, so the location of the remaining Aces and Tens can be deduced late in a deal.
- Partner intent, read from defensive play.

WHERE SKILL ACTS.
- Bid calibration: the fail penalty S+1 heavily punishes overbidding, and underbidding cedes the declarership.
- Choosing Hearts only when the contract is safe.
- Trump choice.
- Card play: smearing Tens to partner, forcing out trumps, timing the last trick worth 10.

CHANCE. I estimate the deal decides roughly 40-50% of the outcome over only 6 deals, which is substantial. A good player is still clearly favoured:
- A weak player who bids greedily or never adjusts loses heavily on failed contracts.
- A strong hand earns little if it is underbid or misplayed.
- A poor hand can be passed to minimise losses.
- Good defence can defeat contracts.

ALL PLAYERS PLAYING WELL. The result then depends partly on the deals, but not on a hidden type or a single draw. Bidding judgement and play still vary the result, so this is luck that good play can overcome, not luck alone.
